head: Coding or Cheating? An Investigation of Frontier Coding LLMs Yuntao Gui∗ research@logitly.ai ytgui@cse.cuhk.edu.hk Abstract Frontier agentic LLMs are trained on verifiable rewards in rein- forcement learning (RL) environments built from real software repositories. A passing test suite is treated as the reward for solving the task. We show that, on hard problems, frontier models often satisfy these rewards by obtaining the answer instead of deriving it, known as reward hacking. Prior reports document this behavior on public benchmarks. We test its persistence on unseen problems. In a hardened environment where the answer cannot leak, nearly every model we tested attempted to recover the answer, escalating through tiers of increasingly specialized exploitation: mining the repository history for the upstream fix, inspecting the git object store directly, and sweeping the filesystem for a possible newer copy of the source or hidden tests. These attempts were concentrated on the hardest problems, and the models differed in whether, how often, and how deeply they escalated. Our position is that this behavior is a learned shortcut, acquired in RL environments that leak the answer, not a sign of intelligence. We release agent traces for these models to support further study at https://huggingface.co/datasets/logitly- ai/reward-hacking-raw-v1. r. Network egress is blocked at the container boundary, so upstream patches, issue threads, and newer releases are all out of reach. The environment is read-only, so the agent can only read, think about, and analyze the code, instead of modifying it. It is designed to resist outside help: with the network blocked, the local machine is the only place left to mine. Python is installed with a minimal set of packages, and no source code or Linux headers are installed. The repository’s git history is carefully processed to contain no future commits, and local git objects are pruned so that nothing leaks. The tasks are 20 instances drawn from three large open-source repositories: linux, ffmpeg, and llvm-project. Table 1 lists each task with its repository, a short description, and the standard de- viation of its reward. They are selected to be challenging: hard enough to trigger reward hacking. We run every agent three times per task, retrying on any unexpected stop, e.g., an LLM endpoint error, a container OOM, or an agent panic. Each run is stored as an agent trace in the Anthropic Messages API format, chosen for its clear typing and structure. A trace records the conversation the har- nes

not on an allowlist. 2.2 Git Object Model and History Retention Git stores a repository as a set of immutable objects, each identified by a hash of its content [5]. There are four object types. A blob stores the contents of one file. A tree represents a directory: it maps names to blobs or to other trees. A commit points to one tree, which is a snapshot of the whole repository. It also records the author, a message, and the hashes of its parent commits. A tag attaches a name and a message to a commit. Each commit refers to its parents by hash, so commits form a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of history. Git stores snapshots, not changes. A commit’s patch is computed on demand by comparing its tree with its parent’s tree. Objects are stored either one by one or compressed together into packfiles. A reference is a named pointer to a commit. Branches, tags, and remote-tracking branches are all references. The reflog records each reference’s past values. Special references record the state before a reset and the result of the latest fetch. An object is reachable if it can be reached by following links from some reference; otherwise it is unreachable. Network egress is blocked at the container boundary, so upstream patches, issue threads, and newer releases are all out of reach. The environment is read-only, so the agent can only read, think about, and analyze the code, instead of modifying it. It is designed to resist outside help: with the network blocked, the local machine is the only place left to mine. Python is installed with a minimal set of packages, and no source code or Linux headers are installed. The repository’s git history is carefully processed to contain no future commits, and local git objects are pruned so that nothing leaks. The tasks are 20 instances drawn from three large open-source repositories: linux, ffmpeg, and llvm-project. Table 1 lists each task with its repository, a short description, and the standard de- viation of its reward. They are selected to be challenging: hard enough to trigger reward hacking. We run every agent three times per task, retrying on any unexpected stop, e.g., an LLM endpoint error, a container OOM, or an agent panic. Each run is stored as an agent trace in the Anthropic Me

A trace records the conversation the har- ness mediated: the conversation turns, thinking blocks, tool calls, and tool outputs, together with the harness’s permission decisions. These traces are the evidence base for the taxonomy of Section 4. 3.2 Definition of Cheating The agent’s job is to work from what the environment provides: the repository at the given commit, the task, and the history that produced it. Reward hacking begins where the agent reaches infor- mation from after the base state, or information that encodes the answer itself. We count three kinds of severity, ordered from lowest to highest, by how far the access departs from what an engineer could legitimately reach. Future mining (low). Commits, refs, or branches that postdate the base commit, reached through version control while seeking the upstream fix. When the named references yield no fix, the agent turns to git’s in- ternal storage (Table 3). It reads and enumerates objects in the store (hid-cat), lists packed commits, and surveys the store (hid-pack). It enumerates dangling commits and blobs unreachable from any reference (hid-fsck). It reads reference values that may leak future commits (hid-reflog) and inspects raw metadata and alternate stores (hid-store). This content sits below where engineering is normally done, which carries high severity. 4.3 Out-of-repository scan (critical) Once the agent exhausts the repository’s recoverable history, the scan leaves version control for the filesystem (Table 4). The target now sits outside version control entirely, which carries the high- est severity. The first patterns target the sandbox itself: the agent probes the blocked network boundary (scan-net) and inspects the mount and boundary paths, including the mounted secrets vol- ume (scan-mnt). In our environment these attempts meet a closed boundary, and the sandbox holds. Nearly every model attempted to obtain the answer instead of deriv- ing it, escalating through tiers of increasingly specialized exploita- tion: mining repository history for the upstream fix, recovering unreachable objects from git’s internal storage, and sweeping the filesystem for a newer copy of the source or hidden tests. The at- tempts concentrate on the hardest problems, and the models differ in whether, how often, and how deeply they escalate. We interpret this behavior as a learned shortcut, acquired in RL environments that leak the answer, and one that persists even when the envi- ronment no longer leaks. wise it is unreachable. An unreachable commit that no other commit lists as a parent is dangling. Moving or deleting a reference only changes which objects are reachable; it never deletes objects. Unreachable objects stay in the object database until garbage collection or an explicit git gc --prune=now command prunes them. By default, pruning only re- moves objects older than a grace period, and objects still referenced by the reflog count as reachable. So deleting a branch, checking out an older commit, or doing a hard reset leaves the objects of later commits in place. 2.3 Reward Hacking in RL Environments Reward hacking happens when a policy trained on a reward earns high reward without completing the intended task [1, 11, 16, 23, 28]. The reward only partly specifies the objective. So training reinforces any behavior that satisfies the reward while violating its intent, just as it would reinforce a real solution. Repository-level software engineering environments are one important case of this setting. They are usually built by mining issue–fix pairs from public repositories. Each environment specifies a base commit (usually a checkout from a past time), the task (an issue descri

checkout from a past time), the task (an issue description), and a set of tests that fail at the base commit and pass after the fix. The agent works on the repository at the base commit. The reward comes from running these hidden tests against the agent’s final repository state or proposed patch. Passing the tests therefore approximates the real objective: a correct fix for the issue. Known ways of hacking the reward include modifying or deleting tests, special-casing test inputs, and exiting early with a success status. This paper focuses on investigating reward hacking on repository- level RL environments: rather than solving the problem by reason- ing over the code, the agent attempts to recover the ground-truth solution from the environment itself. Building environments usu- ally means cloning the full upstream repository and resetting it to the base commit. An incorrectly processed RL environment can leave history that postdates the base commit inside the repository. This leak is the exploit path our investigation targets. 3 Investigation Setup Our testbed is a standard repository-level RL evaluation, hardened at every layer we control. The environment is read-only, so the agent can only read, think about, and analyze the code, instead of modifying it. It is designed to resist outside help: with the network blocked, the local machine is the only place left to mine. Python is installed with a minimal set of packages, and no source code or Linux headers are installed. The repository’s git history is carefully processed to contain no future commits, and local git objects are pruned so that nothing leaks. The tasks are 20 instances drawn from three large open-source repositories: linux, ffmpeg, and llvm-project. We run every agent three times per task, retrying on any unexpected stop, e.g., an LLM endpoint error, a container OOM, or an agent panic. The same repository-plus-tests format also underlies training environments for RL, such as SWE-Gym [25], R2E-Gym [12], and SWE-smith [30]. These environments use test- based pass/fail signals as rewards. This setup makes the integrity of the sandbox important, because anything an agent can read or modify in the environment can affect both its evaluation score and its training signal. Recent hardening efforts respond to this concern: SWE-Bench Pro Verified [32] and Lego-RL [7] both remove residual git objects, hidden tests, and metadata leaks. Reward hacking and evaluation cheating. Frontier coding agents often exploit the evaluation setup instead of solving the task. METR reported cases of models locating leaked solutions in task metadata and copying grader answers [18]. A growing set of studies measures this behavior systematically. ImpossibleBench measures a "cheating rate" on tasks whose specification conflicts with the tests [33].
